title: Human oversight models
summary: Human oversight ranges from approving each action before it happens, through supervising with a stop control, to setting policy and reviewing samples afterwards. The right level follows the action's reversibility, reach and regulatory class, and costs friction.
useIf: You must decide how much a person should be involved in what an AI system or agent does.
avoidIf: You plan to bolt on a yes/no button and call it oversight: approval without evidence or authority is theatre.

explain.md: Three models are in common use, though sources define them loosely, so state your own definitions. **In the loop**: a person approves or makes each decision before it takes effect. **On the loop**: the system acts and a person monitors, with the power to interrupt or stop. **Over the loop**: people set policy and boundaries, then audit logs and review samples afterwards. The same system can mix them by action class: reads run freely, reversible writes are sampled, irreversible actions wait for approval.

Law points the same way. For high-risk systems, EU AI Act Article 14 requires oversight commensurate with risk, autonomy and context. People must be able to understand the system's limits, stay aware of automation bias, interpret outputs, decide not to use or override an output, and interrupt with a stop control. For biometric identification under Annex III point 1(a), two competent people must verify separately before action [[r5]]. Deployers must assign oversight to people with competence, training, authority and support [[tr1]]. Meta's Agents Rule of Two adds a design rule: if a session needs untrusted input, sensitive access and the ability to change state or communicate externally, require human approval or an equivalent [[r23]].

explain.title: Approval is not oversight by itself
explain.md: A reviewer who sees no evidence, has no authority to refuse or is rewarded for speed will approve everything. Show arguments and sources, seed known-bad items and measure the catch rate. The Agent Framework binds a local approval response to a pending request in the same session by default, and `disable_approval_response_binding` opts out [[r16]].

whereToUse: Agents that send email, change records, move money or deploy code
High-risk systems under the EU AI Act, where Article 14 and Article 26 apply
Customer-facing assistants that escalate on low confidence or policy triggers
Bulk automation, using sampled review with an easy undo
Sessions that combine untrusted input, sensitive data and external effects

use: Approve first when actions are irreversible or externally visible
Supervise and escalate when volume is moderate and triggers are reliable
Audit samples when actions are reversible, low-risk and high-volume
Require two reviewers where the law or the stakes demand it
avoid: Approving every low-risk action: reviewers learn to click through
Relying on after-the-fact audit for irreversible harm
Putting oversight on people with no authority or competence to override
flips: The action becomes irreversible: move from sampled audit to approval
Volume rises tenfold: replace blanket approval with risk-tiered gates
The system is classified high-risk: add the Article 14 capabilities and a stop control

pitfalls.symptom: Approval rate is 99.8% and median review time is a few seconds
pitfalls.cause: Rubber-stamping from automation bias, no evidence shown or pressure to clear the queue
pitfalls.fix: Show arguments and sources, seed known-bad items, track catch rate and rotate reviewers

pitfalls.symptom: An approval is replayed or fabricated
pitfalls.cause: Approval responses are not bound to the pending request, user and session
pitfalls.fix: Keep the default binding in Agent Framework and bind approvals to request, user and session [[r16]]

pitfalls.symptom: A write path bypasses the gate
pitfalls.cause: Approval was attached to one tool, not to the action class
pitfalls.fix: Gate by action class and arguments, so another tool cannot cause the same effect

scenarios.title: An agent that emails customers
scenarios.situation: An agent drafts and sends account emails to customers. About 200 emails go out per day. A sent email cannot be recalled.
unknowns: Can the reviewer see the sources and the diff?
How fast must emails go out?
Is any email class low-risk enough to skip approval?
scenarios.question: What oversight model fits?

options.name: Approve before sending, with the draft, recipient and source evidence on screen
options.why: The action is irreversible and public, and 200 per day is a manageable queue.
options.tradeoff: Adds minutes of latency and reviewer time.

options.name: Send first and sample-review afterwards
options.why: A wrong or injected email cannot be taken back.
options.tradeoff: Right for reversible actions such as internal tags.

options.name: Escalate only when the model reports low confidence
options.tradeoff: Model confidence is a weak signal, and a prompt-injected agent can be confident and wrong.

flips.then: Tier by risk: approve high-value or new-recipient emails, template the rest.
Sampled review with an undo is enough.

scenarios.takeaway: Irreversible and external means approve first.

scenarios.title: Bulk tagging of documents
scenarios.situation: An agent applies metadata tags to 50,000 internal documents a day. Tags can be changed at any time and affect search ranking only.
scenarios.question: How much human oversight?

options.name: Sampled review with an easy undo and an alert on drift in tag distribution
options.why: Per-item approval would be impossible and adds little safety for reversible tags.
options.tradeoff: Some wrong tags live until the sample or alert catches them.

options.name: Approve every tag
options.why: 50,000 approvals a day produces rubber-stamping, not safety.
options.tradeoff: Right for a small, high-value set.

options.name: Audit log only
options.tradeoff: No active check, so drift goes unseen.

flips.then: They are no longer low-risk: add approval for permission-affecting tags.

flips.if: Error rate in samples exceeds a threshold

scenarios.takeaway: Reversible and high-volume means sample, with undo.

scenarios.title: A system classed as high-risk
scenarios.situation: A deployer uses an AI system that ranks applicants for a service. The deployer has classified it as high-risk under the EU AI Act. A reviewer currently clicks Accept on the ranking.
unknowns: Do reviewers have competence, training and authority to override?
Are reviewers told how the system can be wrong?
scenarios.question: What do you change?

options.name: Redesign review: show evidence and limits, allow override and stop, assign trained reviewers with authority, log decisions
options.why: Article 14 and 26 expect understanding, awareness of automation bias, override and interruption, with competent and empowered people.

options.name: Keep the Accept button and add an audit log
options.why: A log without real review does not meet the intent of oversight.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable only for non-regulated, low-stakes use.

options.name: Remove the human and publish accuracy numbers
options.why: It drops the oversight the Act expects and shifts risk to affected people.
options.tradeoff: Not a fit for high-risk use.

flips.if: Biometric identification under Annex III point 1(a) is involved
flips.then: Two competent people must verify separately.
Oversight can be lighter, but keep escalation for harm.

scenarios.takeaway: In high-risk use, oversight is a capability, not a button.

quiz.q: Which capabilities does EU AI Act Article 14 expect oversight people to have for high-risk systems?
options: Understand the system's limits and stay aware of automation bias
Decide not to use or override an output
Interrupt the system with a stop control
Approve outputs without access to the reasoning inputs
quiz.explain: Article 14 lists understanding limits, automation-bias awareness, interpretation, override and a stop control. Approving without evidence is the failure it guards against [[r5]].

quiz.q: A review queue shows 99.8% approvals with a median review time of 4 seconds. What is the most likely issue and first fix?
options: The model is perfect: raise volume
Reviewers are too slow: remove review
Rubber-stamping: seed known-bad items and show evidence
quiz.explain: Near-total approval at seconds per item signals automation bias. Seeding bad items measures real catch rate. Perfection is unlikely and removing review drops the control.

quiz.q: Which change most clearly moves an action from sampled audit to approve-first?
options: The action becomes irreversible or externally visible
The model gets a higher benchmark score
quiz.explain: Reversibility and reach choose the family of brake. Volume adjusts it, and benchmark scores do not change blast radius.

flashcards.front: In, on and over the loop?
flashcards.back: In: a person approves each decision. On: the system acts and a person can interrupt. Over: people set policy and audit samples afterwards. Definitions vary by source.

flashcards.front: What does Article 14 require of oversight people?
flashcards.back: Understand limits, stay aware of automation bias, interpret output, override and interrupt with a stop control. Two competent people for Annex III point 1(a).

flashcards.front: What is the Agents Rule of Two?
flashcards.back: In one session, avoid combining untrusted input, sensitive access and external effects. If all three are needed, require human approval.
